summary: Defines two X.509 v3 certificate extensions, one binding IP address blocks to a certificate's subject and one binding autonomous system numbers. They convey the subject's authorization to use those resources.

plainLanguage.summary: A digital ID can say which internet addresses and network numbers its owner is in charge of.

questions: what does the inherit element mean in an ip address delegation extension
why does rfc 3779 not use attribute certificates
subtitle: Two certificate extensions that say which IP address blocks and AS numbers a key holder may use.

tldr.problem: There was no scalable way to verify that an organization has the right to use a set of IP address blocks or autonomous system identifiers, for example before trusting a routing announcement.
tldr.mechanism: Two X.509 v3 certificate extensions bind a list of IP address blocks, or a list of AS identifiers, to the certificate subject. Each certificate in a chain may only hold resources that its issuer's certificate also holds.
tldr.outcome: Certificates carrying these extensions work like capabilities: they show that the private key holder is authorized to use the listed resources, and they can be checked by routing protocols such as Secure BGP.

today: RFC 3779 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Certificates for Internet Resources
sections.content:
RFC 3779 defines two X.509 v3 certificate extensions. One binds a list of IP address blocks, often written as prefixes, to the subject (the private key holder) of a certificate. The other binds a list of autonomous system (AS) identifiers to the subject.

The issuer is an entity with the authority to transfer custodianship of the resources: IANA, a regional Internet registry (RIR) or an ISP. The extensions therefore authorize the transfer of the right-to-use from IANA through the RIRs to ISPs and user organizations. The RFC says they may be used by routing protocols such as Secure BGP to verify routing information, or by Internet routing registries to verify the data they receive.

Sections 2 and 3 set encoding rules that MUST be followed. They give each extension a unique encoding that can be compared octet by octet, keep it as small as possible, and let a relying party validate in one pass without sorting or handling adjacent, overlapping or subsumed ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine the internet's address book is handed down from one big office to smaller offices. These certificates are the signed notes that prove who was given which pages.

sections.title: Encoding Addresses, Prefixes and Ranges
sections.content:
An address prefix is a set of 2^k contiguous addresses whose most-significant bits are identical. For example, 10.5.0.0 through 10.5.1.255 is 512 IPv4 addresses sharing the same 23 leading bits, written 10.5.0.0/23.

In the extension, an address or prefix is a DER-encoded ASN.1 BIT STRING holding only the constant leading bits. The first value octet says how many bits of the last octet are unused, and DER requires those unused bits to be zero. The prefix 10.5.0/23 uses three octets but only 23 bits, so its initial octet is 1.

A range is a SEQUENCE of the lowest and highest address, each as a bit string. The lowest address has its trailing zero bits removed, and the highest has its trailing one bits removed. A prefix can always be expressed as a range, but a range cannot always be expressed as a prefix. The special case of all addresses, 0/0, is encoded with a length octet of one, an initial octet of zero and no subsequent octets.

Trailing zero bits matter for prefixes: 10.64/12 and 10.64.0/20 have different encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing every house number on a street, you write the part they all share, like saying 'everything starting with 10.5'. A range is for when a neat shared start does not fit.

sections.title: The IP Address Delegation Extension
sections.content:
The extension is identified by id-pe-ipAddrBlocks, defined as { id-pe 7 }. It SHOULD be marked CRITICAL, so that a relying party must understand it before using the certificate for the purpose it was issued.

Its value, IPAddrBlocks, is a sequence of IPAddressFamily entries. Each has an addressFamily (a two-octet Address Family Identifier, optionally followed by a one-octet SAFI) and an ipAddressChoice. There MUST be only one entry per AFI and SAFI combination, entries MUST be in ascending order, and IPv4 (AFI 0001) comes before IPv6 (AFI 0002).

The choice is either inherit, meaning the addresses come from the issuer's certificate (or its issuer's, recursively), or addressesOrRanges, a sorted list of prefixes and ranges. Entries MUST NOT overlap, and contiguous entries MUST be combined into a single range or, whenever possible, a single prefix. Sorting uses the lowest address followed by the prefix length, not the raw DER bytes. Any range that can be a prefix MUST be encoded as a prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate holds a tidy list: first the old-style addresses, then the new-style ones, each sorted and with no overlaps. Or it can say 'use whatever my boss had'.

sections.title: The AS Identifier Delegation Extension
sections.content:
The second extension carries autonomous system identifiers and uses id-pe-autonomousSysIds, defined as { id-pe 8 }. Like the first, it SHOULD be CRITICAL. An autonomous system is a set of routers under a single technical administration, and an AS number is a 32-bit number identifying it.

The value, ASIdentifiers, can hold up to two lists: asnum for AS numbers (used by BGP) and rdi for routing domain identifiers (specified for IDRP). If both appear, asnum MUST come first. Each list is either inherit or a sequence of single identifiers and min to max ranges.

The ordering rules mirror those for addresses: entries MUST NOT overlap, MUST be sorted by increasing numeric value, and contiguous identifiers MUST be combined into a single range whenever possible. The RFC adds that using the extension is not meant to change how AS identifiers are managed.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the same kind of note, but for network ID numbers instead of addresses: a sorted list of numbers and number ranges the owner may use.

sections.title: Certification Path Validation
sections.content:
Both extensions add a rule to normal certification path validation. As each certificate in a path is validated, the resources in its extension MUST be subsumed by (fully contained in) the resources in the issuer's certificate. Validation MUST fail when this is not the case.

The trust anchor, and every certificate along the path, MUST contain the extension. The initial set of allowed address ranges, or AS identifiers, is taken from the trust anchor certificate. The same rule is stated separately for the AS identifier extension in Section 3.3.

The sorted, non-overlapping, minimal encodings from Section 1 exist so this subset check can be done in a single pass.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper can only hand out what it was given. If a certificate claims something its parent never had, the check fails.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because X.509 certificates are digitally signed, no extra integrity service is needed. These certificates need not be kept secret, and unrestricted, anonymous access to them has no security implications.

The extensions express authorization: a right-to-use for IP addresses or AS identifiers. They were developed to support a secure version of BGP, but may be used elsewhere. In that setting the certificates function as capabilities, asserting that the holder of the private key is authorized to use the listed resources. As a result the Subject field is largely irrelevant for security purposes, contrary to common PKI conventions. The RFC also notes that security factors outside its scope affect the assurance users get.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate is like a key that opens a particular door. What matters is who holds the key, not what name is written on the tag.

sections.title: Why Not Attribute Certificates
sections.content:
Appendix D explains why the authors put the authorization in ordinary public key certificates rather than in separate X.509 attribute certificates (ACs, RFC 3281). The usual reasons for ACs do not apply here. The certificates are issued only for authorization, so their lifetime matches the authorization, and the issuer is authoritative for the resources. The Subject name may even be randomly assigned by the issuing CA, giving the resource holder limited anonymity.

The appendix also lists mismatches with RFC 3281. That RFC does not recommend AC chains, but allocation from IANA to RIRs to ISPs needs chains. An AC issuer cannot also be a CA, which would roughly double the number of certificate issuers and CRLs. And an AC issuer must be directly trusted, which does not scale across thousands of ISPs, whereas a single PKI with a trusted root does.
sections.plainLanguage: They could have used a second kind of card, but that would mean carrying two cards and twice as many offices to run. One card is simpler.
